output:
**The house in Glenmore**

Úna set this blog up years ago so the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds could keep up with us. I’ve been glad of it more times than I’ve said, and I’ve been poor at using it. I’m going to use it properly now. I have something to tell you, and I want to tell it once, myself, in full, rather than have it go round in bits from phone to phone.

I have agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore, the old Mulkerrin place near Oughterard. Tom’s grandfather Pádraig Mulkerrin built it in 1931. Tom grew up there. Tom died in March 2024. Since then I’ve been driving out every fortnight — forty minutes each way — to air it and check the pipes. The sale was agreed on 3 November and it closes on 15 January 2027. I want that date sitting plainly in this post, so that nobody hears it from someone else again.

Some of you heard it second-hand before I’d told you properly. That is my fault. I am sorry for how you found out. I am not sorry for the decision. Both of those things are true, and I’m not going to pretend one cancels out the other.

I handled it badly. I told myself I was waiting until the sale was certain, and then I told myself I was waiting until I had the words right. Neither was the real reason. The real reason is that I did not want to face all of you with it. I spent my working life teaching primary school and telling children to use their words, and here I am at seventy-one, needing to take my own advice.

Declan heard it from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp, not from me. He rang at two in the morning his time. He said I was “selling Dad.” I said things back I shouldn’t have. I’m not going to repeat them here. They were said to wound, and I’d say they did. I regret them.

Declan, I know you read these. I want you to hear this directly from me: I am not angry with you. I don’t think you’re wrong to be upset. I regret not consulting you. I should have talked to you before I decided anything. You are Tom’s son, and your voice should have been in it. I didn’t do that. But I am not willing to wait until your summer visit. I can’t put the house on hold until summer, and I won’t pretend that waiting would make this easier. That is not meant as a criticism of you. It is where I have got to. The door here is open to you. It will stay open. I mean that.

This is not an apology for selling the house. It is an explanation, and an apology for the way you heard. I’m not asking for anyone’s blessing. I’m asking you to hear it from me, once.

Some of you will ask why now. There are practical things, and I’ll put them down plainly, because I’d rather you had them than a vague version. In September I had Ó Flaithearta’s out to look at the roof. The slates need attention and so does the back chimney. The quote was €38,000. There is damp in the back bedroom on top of that. The septic tank needs replacing to sell to anyone anyway. Those are not the only reasons, but they are real. I’m not going to dress this up like a notice in the paper. The roof is €38,000, and it’s an old house, and there would be more after that.

I could spend the money. Maybe I could. But I would be spending it to keep a house I can’t keep up, and I would still be driving out every fortnight to check the pipes.

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door. There was frost. I lay there twenty minutes before I could get up. I told nobody until now. I was lucky. I know I was lucky. But since then I am afraid of being alone at the house. I don’t mean I’m frightened of shadows. I mean I’m frightened of the step, and the frost, and the phone being in the other room. I cannot go on maintaining it. I’m not helpless, but I’m not a young woman either, and the house wants more than I have.

I know what the house means. I don’t need to be told. I was proposed to in the haggard behind it in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. Our children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan wouldn’t come out until his lips were blue. Those things don’t go with the deed. They never could. But they are not arguments for keeping a roof over a house that no longer has a family living in it.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I have thought about that more than anything else. The people buying it are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They have two small children. They want to live in it, not turn it into a holiday let. That mattered to me. It mattered more than the money.

There were people from Dublin in the summer who offered more. I took the lower offer on purpose. The price was fair. I wasn’t taken advantage of, and I didn’t sell it cheap to be done with it. I chose them. I’m not going to pretend I know them well. I don’t. But I know what they want it for, and it’s the same thing Tom wanted for it.

I’m keeping the dresser. It’s going to Úna’s. I’m keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp, and the gate sign. I’m not clearing the history out with the furniture. The Joyces have said family can come out and walk the land any time. I hope in time you will.

Before it’s cleared, we’re having a day out at the house on Sunday 13 December. Anyone who can make it, come. Soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies. It won’t be a formal occasion. I’d rather see you there than have this post be the last word on it. If you can’t come, I understand. It’s a long way from Perth and Boston and Leeds. But the invitation is real.

I’m not going to pretend I’ve handled this well. I haven’t. I let the news travel before I gave it to you properly, and that was a poor way to treat family. I regret not consulting Declan most of all. But I am not willing to wait until the summer, and I am not going to apologise for a decision I believe is right.

Over the best part of two years I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. That has been a hard thing to learn. I’m still learning it. There is relief in it too, and I’m not proud of that, but it’s there. I don’t expect everyone to feel the same. I only ask that you hear it from me.

The sale closes on 15 January 2027. The day out is Sunday 13 December. The door is open. I’ll see you at the house if you can come.
